speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext:
I wish at this juncture
to rise to a question both of privilege and of order. Rule 37 of this House covers the procedure which must be followed both in the case of questions and in the case of answers. That rule reads:
Questions may be put to ministers of the crown relating to public affairs; and to members, relating to any bill, motion, or other public matter connected with the business of the House, in which such members may be concerned; but in putting any such question or in replying to the same no argument or opinion is to be offered, nor any facts stated, except so far as may be necessary to explain the same. And in answering any such question the matter to which the same refers shall not be debated.
In the light of this rule I beg to make reference to a question put and an answer given in this House on April 2. The question is put by the hon. member for Kent, New Brunswick (Mr. Doucet) and, with the answer, appears at page 1780 of Hansard as follows:
Mr. Doucet:
1.	What was the amount paid by the government in connection with the investigation and report made by Sir Henry Drayton in regard to the North Atlantic Steamship Conference and ocean rates?
It is to that question I refer, but I may as well read the second question although it is irrelevant:
2.	What is the amount already paid and payable to Mr. W. T. R. Preston in connection with his investigation and report with the said matters?
I shall repeat the first question upon which I base my objection, together with the answer as given by the Secretary of State (Mr. Copp). They are:
1. What was the amount paid by the government In connection with the investigation and report made by Sir Henry Drayton in regard to the North Atlantic Steamship Conference and ocean rates?
Hon. Mr. Copp:
1. Sir Henry Drayton was carried on the paylist of the Board of Railway Commissioners for the period from July 31, 1913, to September 21, 1913, when he was employed on the ocean rates inquiry, and he was paid during the inquiry his regular salary rate as chief commissioner, namely $12,500 per annum, and $1,074 expenses.
I again, desire to read the rule relating to this matter:
(1) Questions may be put to ministers of the crown relating to public affairs; and to other members, relating to any bill, motion, or other public matter connected with the business of the House, in which such members may be concerned; but in putting any such question or in replying to the same no argument or opinion is to be offered, nor any facts stated, except so far as may be necessary to explain the sacpe. And in answering any such question the matter to which the same refers shall not be debated.
First of all, I would observe that no answer is given to the question as asked. The government, of course, may refuse to answer the question; I do not contend that it is bound to answer it. But if it does answer it is
Privilege-Mr. Meighen

bound to state the facts, and the government, under the rule I have just read, had no right to make a statement which is entirely aside from the answer and not explanatory thereof. In the first place, there is no answer in the present instance of which anything could be explanatory; consequently, this alleged answer is beyond the rule. I submit therefore that it should be expunged. The government was bound, in reply to the question asked, if it answered at all, to state the fact, which is that Sir Henry Drayton got nothing whatever for his services in connection with that inquiry; nor did any other payment made to him in connection with his regular work as chief of the Board of Railway Commissioners have the slightest relation to, much less was it explanatory of, the fact that he got nothing for this particular work. The attempted answer, the gratuitous reference to his being on the paylist, is all the more ungracious when we remember that not only was this work done by him in his holiday time on the railway board and free to the country, but that later his entire work in connection with the Drayton-Aeworth report, which was the basis of the railway policy followed by the administration and which was a prodigious achievement, was also done entirely free of charge. Indeed, a cheque for $15,000 having been sent to him was returned. The same is true in regard to the work done by him as power, light and electricity controller for a long period in 1917-18 and, as well, as controller of food transports. These services . were all given without remuneration, and in the face of that I think that the government, apart from what its legal right may have been, was most ungracious and unfair in this reply. I appeal to you, Mr. Speaker, as having supervision over both questions and answers, to see that they come within the rule; that supervision is given you, Sir, under the rule of this House which I have cited. I appeal to you to ordler that this supposed answer be stricken out and that question No. 1 be restored.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext:
I quite agree with my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) that the habit of putting questions asking for opinions of all kinds, including opinions on matters of law, has become altogether too frequent of late. But I cannot follow the hon. member in his argument as to the irrelevancy of the answer given to the question:

What was the amount paid by the government in connection with the investigation and report made by Sir Henry Drayton in regard to the North Atlantic Steamship Conference and ocean rates?
This question was only one means by which the House and the country could ascertain what amount of money had been paid the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) in a certain capacity, and the answer as given in Hansard is merely a statement of actual facts. Questions are put to the government in order that information may be searched for; and that is the only way that information can be got. The mere statement of the fact that the hon. member was at that time a member of the Board of Railway Commissioners in receipt of a salary of $12,000 or so a year-which I assume would indicate that he must have been available for the government of the day for any special work of the kind referred to-does not constitute any assertion of opinion on the part of the government, nor is it any violation of the particular rule applicable to this case. As to the information in regard to the question relating to expenses paid, that I think is perfectly proper. And the answer is given to it. It seems to me that my right hon. friend is unnecessarily worrying over this matter. No answer given by the government is intended in any way to reflect upon the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), nor does it in my opinion constitute any argument or expression of opinion; it is merely a statement of fact. The answer in this instance is simply the statement that the hon. member received a certain salary and certain expenses in his capacity as Chief Commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext: The only statement made by my hon. friend which is pertinent to the argument I sought to advance is this, that the hon. member for West York having been at the time a railway commissioner in receipt of a certain salary, he was available-as the hon. member "assumed"-for any other services the government wished him to perform. The hon. member could not assume any such thing. Sir Henry Drayton was employed as railway commissioner by this country. Those were his duties, and those alone, within the compass of his salary. Consequently that assertion was not correct. He was not to be available at all. His services were given gratuitously.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext: He became available.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext:
He made himself available, but the fact that he was railway com-

Privilege-Mr. Meighen
missioner had nothing whatever to do with his claim for remuneration. My point is this: The correct answer to the question was, "Nothing." What is stated here can only be justified as an explanation of an answer. There is no answer given to explain. If it had been given, it is no explanation. It has nothing at all to do with the fact.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext:
That is a
question of opinion.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext:
It is not a question
of opinion at all. A man is employed to do certain work. When he does that work he earns the salary assigned. I think the government would have been better advised to admit the hasty reply, agree to expunge this from the record, and give the right answer.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I for one fail to follow my right hon. friend in the trend of his argument on this point. Nobody will deny that the hon. member in whose behalf he spoke is very deserving of consideration for the services he rendered, but the question being put as it was "What was the amount paid by the government in connection with the investigation and report made by Sir Henry Drayton?-I do not believe that a clearer answer and one more to the point could have been given than the one that was given, which says in effect that from the 31st of July to the 21st of September, 1913, Sir Henry Drayton was carried on the pay sheet of the railway commissioners of Canada, and as such received his ordinary salary of $12,500. I think the question being put as it was, the country was entitled to know what was the remuneration paid to Sir Henry Drayton, and the answer is to the effect that he was employed from the 31st of July to the 21st of September, 1913, and that while he was employed on the Ocean Rates inquiry he was paid during that inquiry his regular salary as chief commissioner, which was $12,500. I do not think there is any room for dispute in respect to that. The answer was directly to the point, and I do not think it gives occasion to raise either a point of order or a question of privilege. I for one am fully satisfied that the answer covers the question, and that it is an answer in fact to a question of fact.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext:
I think perhaps the answer covers the question, but more is given than is actually necessary in answering the question. It was not necessary in making that reply to state the salary Sir Henry Drayton was receiving as railway commissioner. A proper answer, if I may venture to suggest it, would, have been to state
simply that he was commissioner of railways at that time, and that he received no further remuneration for his services on this inquiry, except his travelling and other expenses here set out. It is framed a little awkwardly, perhaps not intentionally; I think it could have been framed in better words than are used. It is quite easily understood in reading the answer what the faets were, but there is more said in the reply, I think, than was really necessary.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend suggests as an objection to the answer that it states What the salary of Sir Henry Drayton was, surely he will not think there was anything wrong in that, because the way questions are being put in the House, the very next question might have been: " What was the salary of Sir Henry Drayton at that time?"

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext: That is not pertinent to the question. No one was asking what his salary was.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext: The question was, what was the amount paid?

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MEIGHEN POINT OF ORDER-FORM OF ANSWER TO A QUESTION
speechtext: I hold no brief whatever for the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), but I do not think that justice has been done him in the way the answer has been given to this question. Sir Henry Drayton, it appears, gave his services in connection with this inquiry at a time when he was on his holidays. He is now back in political life, and that has a bearing on the matter. If a man did that much gratis, for his country, I think he has the right to get the credit for it, or at least it is only fair that the public should know on what conditions he gave this service. But by making the statement that he was drawing his salary as a railway commissioner, as the answer does, it implies that during this inquiry he was serving his time as railway commissioner and getting paid for it. Technically, perhaps, the government has answered aright, but I think there is a further explanation coming to Sir Henry Drayton. I think there is more in what has not been said in the reply, than in what was said. I think the explanation should have been fully and impartially given. The answer that was given was a biased answer, in my opinion. I do not think justice was done to the hon. member.

The attack has been made upon the government that it has not raised the duties- not that it has not sufficiently lowered them. The attacks by the Conservative party are based on the charge that the government has not raised the duties although they say it should have done so, and a good deal of argument has been addressed to the farmers of this country in that connection. They are told that they are being betrayed and badly treated by this government because it has refused to put up the duties on agricultural products. Well, I am not going to emulate the fashion in which the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) has addressed the House; I am not going to talk of gold bricks, or of shell games, or anything of that sort; but I say this: that any attempt to pretend that the farmers, as a whole, can be benefited by the imposition of duties upon what they produce and of which they have a large exportable surplus i3 a cruel deception, it is something which

cannot be done. The House will forgive me if I deal with this at some little length because it is a matter of real importance to this country.
The farmers should not be allowed to believe that they can be helped by the imposition of a protective duty on what they have to produce, because as long as this country has a vast exportable surplus of agricultural products to send to the markets of the world the price which we get in those markets for that surplus is what determines the price of the entire production. There may be cases here and there where the contrary obtains, there may be a few market gardeners near some large city who by means of the duties are able to get a little higher price at certain times of the year for what they have got to supply to their neighbours who live in the adjacent city. That may be true, but we are not here to look after special interests, we are here to look after the general interests; and so I say that the farmer cannot be benefited by a protective tariff. Now I am going to quote evidence not from Canada first but from the United States, because I take it I am in the sense of this House when I say that if that has proven to be impossible in the United States, if responsible people in the United States say it cannot be done in that country-which has in comparison to its production a far smaller exportable surplus than we have-then a fortiori it cannot be done in Canada. The first witness I will call in this regard is the man who was Democratic candidate for the position of president at the last election, and he spoke on September 7th, 1924, as follows:
In order to delude the farmer with a false pretense of imaginary benefits and with utter disregard of economic law, those in control of the Republican party announced, in the Spring of 1921, that all his ills would be promptly cured by the enactment of a protective tariff for his benefit. They declared that high tariff rates on wheat, corn, livestock, meat products and so forth, would immediately raise the domestic price. Such a law as accordingly placed upon the statute books in May, 1921, but when wheat fell from $1.47 in May to $1 in December, and corn from 62 cents in May to 47 cents in October, the promised relief was seen to be a pure political fiction.
Under cover of this pretense, however, the oppressive Fordney-McCumber bill was enacted in September, 1922. Lobbies representing greedy manufacturers stormed the nation's capital and wrote their own excessive and extortionate rates in utter disregard of every theory, even of protective tariff taxation. No consideration was given to the new and changed financial business and economic conditions.
Then further referring to the Fordney-McCumber law he said:
This law is both a fence and an offense. It was a fence against reciprocal trade, no matter how profitable or desirable and shattered our trade structure

'The Budget-Mr. McMaster
throughout the world. It was an offense to every consumer in the United States, and not least of all to the farmers who were left outside the scope of its pretended benefits. It might have been appropriate^ entitled "An act to obstruct our foreign commerce, to increase the prices of what the farmer buys and to reduce the prices of what he sells."
Thereafter, as an additional sop to the farmer, under the so-called flexible provision the duty on wheat was increased by Executive order and that ungrateful commodity promptly responded by a further fall in value. Surely the day when the farmer can be lulled to rest by a nominal tariff on the commodities of which he has a surplus to sell abroad has passed forever.
That is the argument made by the gentleman who presented himself as the presidential candidate of the great Democratic party, a gentleman distinguished at the bar of New York, a gentleman who represented his country at the Court of 'St. James in England, and possibly as attractive a candidate as appeared in the last election before the American people. But those were not only the views of the Democratic party but also the views of the Republican party, or at least of that section of the party who agreed with their vice-presidential candidate Colonel Dawes. He says:
It is an admitted fact that in the case of any agricultural commodity of which we raise a substantial surplus, the price obtainable for this surplus in the world's markets establishes in a general way the price level of the entire crop.
This is from the address delivered by Colonel Dawes, the Republican nominee for the office of vice-president' at Lincoln, Nebraska, in August or September, 1924. But let me quote what I might term a collective witness. In the United States within the last few months a national association of commissioners, secretaries and departments of agriculture gathered together and they held a meeting on the 2nd December, 1924, and I quote the following:
The protective principle affects only those farm crops of which we produce less than we consume, examples of which are wool, flax and sugar. In the case of those crops of which there is an exportable surplus the case is quite different. The price of the exportable surplus is fixed by world-wide competition and is unaffected by a so-called protective tariff. The price level of exportable surplus in turn determines the price level of all that portion of the commodity required for domestic consumption. It is apparent, therefore, that the producer of these farm crops having a surplus available for export, sells at price levels determined by world-wide competition, buys in a market restricted by the operation of the protective principles. Examples are: wheat, corn, pork, and to some extent dairy products.
I also quote figures which appear in the Congressional Record, January 21, 1925, as follows:
Net loss to farmers of United States due to tariff:
Gross cost to farmers	 $426,000,000
Gains to farmers as producers	 125,000,000
Net cost to agriculture	 301,000,000
Now if that is true in the United States it is a great deal truer in Canada.
Will my hon. friend state who asked for protection for the farmers in the United States?

I think the farmers of the United States have been thoroughly fooled by the Republican party ever since the Civil war. They have been asking for protection and they have been getting it, and it has not done them on the whole the slightest bit of good, and it has enabled the protected manufacturers of the country to gouge the people of the United States.

If the exportable surplus determines the price of the home market, how does the hon. member account for the fact that the United States had a surplus production in fruit that they dumped into Canada at a much lower price than the home market? That is why we have an antidumping law.

They are able in that case, I presume by some sort of combination, to maintain their home prices. But I say this: that you might in certain parts of the country find markets which might be rarely helped by the protective principle; but I vas laying down the general principle which is true. It may suffer exceptions in the case of spring strawberries and other things at other times in different parts of the country. But I say as a general rule,-and in our fiscal policy we must be governed by general rules-it is true as a general principle. I appeal to my hon. friend who wishes to be fair to examine these things carefully, and I ask him to open any newspaper which quotes the prices of wheat in Liverpool and the price in Winnipeg, and he will find that the price in Liverpool will be the price at the head of the lakes, plus the cost of transportation. There have been fluctuations in the price of wheat which may have disturbed market conditions, but I say that at almost all times-and I appeal to those hon. members in this House who know more about marketing wheat than I do-you will find the cost of wheat in Great Britain is the cost of wheat at the head of the lakes, plus the cost of transportation to Liverpool.

Is not the fallacy of the
free trade argument the fact that there are so many barriers in the country that they are artificial interferences continually with trade and exportable surpluses and everything else, and you have to deal with it in a practical way in each particular case?

The Budget-Mr. McMnster

This is not a new argument. It was answered by Sir Robert Peel in the forties in the House of Commons, England. He said the best thing Great Britain could do in the face of tariff walls against her was to have a policy of free imports. The fact that you are interfered with when you go to sell is no reason why you should interfere with yourself when you come to buy. It is quite true that the protectionist tariff wall hurts us when we go into other countries to sell. It increases the cost to the consumer in the country to which we are taking our goods, and therefore decreases the demand. It is a hurtful thing to us, but let me give this specific illustration. I know that we free traders are often called theorists, but it is the protectionist who is the theorist. The free trader wants to consider things as they really are. A great many people in my county sell cream in Boston. It is true they have to pay a duty on the cream that goes in. It is paid by the American consumer of that cream. But if there were not a duty there would be a bigger demand for that cream, and therefore the duty hurts the farmer who exports cream from Brome. But is the fact that he is hurt when he is an exporter of cream any reason why he should hurt himself by raising the duties against himself when he wants to buy things which come from the United States?
Does the hon. member say the incidence of tariff taxation always falls upon the consumer in the country to which the article is exported.

No, it depends on how
keen the demand is. If I am trying to place my goods in a protected market, have got to get the goods in there, and it is the only available market, and the demand is not keen, I may in some cases pay the whole duty, or pay part of the duty, in order to get into the market. But I will always be looking for another market, and I think it will be found generally that the incidence of the tax usually falls upon the consumer. It would not be any use to be a protectionist unless that were true. If the exporter to a protected country paid the duty then there would be no protection for the home manufacturer. He would have to compete with the free trade price just the same as before.
Is my hon. friend serious about that?

That is absolutely true, and if my hon. friend with the smiling countenance would consider for a moment, he would see that it was true. Take woollens coming into Canada purchased by Green-

shields, in a case where the British manufacturer so much desired to send the goods to Greenshields that he paid the 25 per cent duty, and that Greenshields was able to buy the British woollens just the same as if the duty was not on at all, what change would the Canadian manufacturer have? He would be compelled to put out a better line of goods to get Greenshields to buy from him, when Greenshields could buy from the British firm without paying any duty.

I am delighted
with my hon. friend's statement, and I am going to ask him another question. Does he think-and I followed him very closely- that the illustration that he is applying as to the reflex action in the domestic market of the outside cost of wheat would apply simi'larly as regards any other commodity in the would?

I think so. Our Dairy
Commissioner, Mr. Ruddick, says that the price of dairy produce is, on the whole, governed by precisely the same rule. I say that wheat is the classic example of the theory which I am enunciating to this House. We examined that question with great care some two or three years ago in the agricultural committee.

I think it is
not the example, it is the one exception. But perhaps >my hon. friend will tell me as to the price of butter in New York as against the price of butter in any centre he desires to pick in Canada. I think he will find his principle does not work.

Of course, when you
come to retail prices-
Wholesale.

I think you will find
wholesale prices will be much more on an equality than retail prices because retail prices may vary from store to store. But I say this-and I believe I am correct when I say it-that if you have a great surplus for export, the price you get for that exportable surplus will determine, both generally as regards volume and generally in point of time, the price you have to accept for your home production.

Supposing an exportable
surplus from the United States was dumped into Canada at a price below that at which the goods can be produced in either Canada or the United States, would that be in the interest generally of the people of this country ?

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
Mr. M'cMASTER:	That would depend
whether it was done continuously or not. If it was done continuously at a price lower than that at which we could produce the goods, I believe it would be greatly in our interest to get that and to devote our attention to producing something else.

It would be intermittent,
but enough to hurt business in this country.

I believe, in the long
run, less harm would be done to the vast majority of the people of Canada whose interest we have to think of first, namely, the consumers, by allowing them to get the advantage of even such intermittent dumping as my hon. friend suggests.

The hon.
member in his very interesting discussion quoted figures, I think, to show that the net cost to agriculture in the United States of the tariff was $301,000,000. Does the hon. member mean that to be the net cost of the protective principle as applied in the United States or the net cost of simply the agricultural protection?

The figures which I
have before me purport to show that the gross cost to the farmers of the protective principle is $426,000,000; that, in other words, what they have to buy has been artificially increased in price to the extent of $426,000,000; that the price of what they have to sell has been artificially increased to the extent of $125,000,000, and that, therefore, the net cost to agriculture is $301,000,000. That is dealing only with the matter in the large. That does not take into account the fact, I think, that the wheat farmer in the United States is not helped much by protection. He may be occasionally, but as a rule he is not helpfrd by protection. Therefore, there is really no gain in protection for him at all. The United States exports, if I mistake not, about three bales of cotton for every four she produces, so that the price of cotton in the United States is unaffected by a tariff, and the cotton farmer, the farmer who grows only cotton, cannot be helped at all' by a protective tariff. Therefore, he has to bear his share of the loss. This purports to give agriculture, as a whole, and tends to show, if these estimates are correct, that even in the highly industrialized United States, where, I think, the proportion of urban population to rural population is much greater than with us, the protective principle is disadvantageous to the farming interests.
Whose estimates are these? Where can we get them and where are they made up?

The whole matter is
thoroughly discussed in the Congressional Record of the 21st January, 1925, just at the beginning.

What number of years
would these figures cover?

I am unable to state,
but it is a very recent compilation and a compilation which, I take it, was induced by the very disturbed condition of agriculture in the United States a year or two ago.

That was the net loss per
annum, was it not?

That was supposed to be the net loss per annum. Of course it is a mere computation, a mere estimate; but the point I wish to emphasize to this House is that even in the United States where, if in any place on this continent, the protective principle should be able to help the farmer, according to this authority it does nothing of the sort.
The next point which I wish to bring up is the argument made by protectionists that importations from abroad of goods diminish the demand for labour in Canada. We heard a great deal about how much more prosperous we would be if we could only 5 p.m. shut goods out, and the inference was, in fact the assertion was made, that the Canadian wage earner would be more prosperous under a protective tariff than he would be if a protective tariff did not exist. That is a fallacy and I will endeavour to prove my statement. You may possibly help one special line of industry by protection; you may possibly help the men who are engaged in that particular line of industry by protection; but you cannot help industry or labour as a whole by protection and I will tell you why. What labour can get out of industry by way of either salary or wages is governed, first of all, by the wealth which is produced in the country. If a great deal of wealth is produced in a country, there is more to be divided between the capitalists and the workers. Of course protection cannot increase the wealth of the country. It can only direct labour and capital into certain channels rather than others. I think history shows and economics teach that it is more likely to misdirect than properly to direct labour and capital into channels away from those into which they would otherwise flow.

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
Let me place this before the House. Protection, as a whole and generally speaking, will raise prices. If a man can save a dollar or two dollars on a pair of shoes and a woman two or three dollars on a dress, what are they going to do with that money? They are going to buy other things with it. They are going to create other demands and these other demands will have to be met by labour. Therefore, the more natural you get the channel in which labour and capital flow the more you force labour and capital into channels which will produce the greatest economic return, the greater will be your wealth and the greater will be the return for labour. I need not stress the point. I believe it to be sound.
Now, I have talked a long time and I mingled praise with blame, and perhaps the House will say, "You have spoken for an hour and a half; what have you practical to suggest?" Well, with all respect to this House, I am going to make a few practical suggestions. Our tariff problem, our railway problem, our immigration problem are inextricably mingled together; they all form parts of a larger problem-'the condition-of-Canada problem. We want better conditions in Canada, and these problems, tariff, immigration, railway, are merely aspects of the one great problem. The government has proposed a tariff board. Well, a tariff board may be useful in getting certain information, but it will not determine, or it should not be allowed to determine, the policy of the country. This policy must be determined by the representatives of the people. It seems to me that what we must determine, before we can have a tariff board functioning usefully for us, is whether we are going to have a tariff which is primarily for the purpose of raising revenue, or primarily for the purpose of affording protection; because it cannot be properly designed to do both. Now, I hope that when the tariff board is chosen it will direct itself to the examination of the question:	How we can raise more
revenue through the tariff with the least dislocation of business and on the soundest principles of business and economics.

Will the hon.
member allow me a question on that point? Has he considered the figures collected by the American government under their advanced and present high rates as against the figures that were collected before the emergency tariff?
No.

One is the
multiple of the other.

But I have read a
good deal as to the amount of dissatisfaction there is with the tariff board of the United States; how that tariff board has not prevented scandals, such as their woollen schedule K, which is a crime and a disgrace to any civilized country; how that tariff board is not recommending against the continuation of high duties in industries where by the application of automatic machinery and other labour saving devices the United States are able to compete on an equal footing with the' whole world. I would pray the government in this regard not to establish a highly organized board with chairman, vicechairman and commissioners and with a staff of stenographers and clerks; I implore them not to do that because when those gentlemen are appointed-if they are-their whole subconscious desire will be to maintain protection in order to retain their jobs and because no man when put in a position of that sort can refrain from trying to magnify his office. There are, however, men in the employ of the government whose fund of information and whose collection of data would be a great benefit to anyone who may be called1 upon to deal with the tariff question. I do not think I am going beyond the bounds of propriety when I say that a member of this tariff board should be our Dominion Statistician who, I think, knows more about the condition of trade and industry in this country than possibly any other man within the confines of the Dominion.
Now I am going to speak for a moment about immigration. The needs of the Canadian people in this regard demand such arrangements or rearrangements within the cabinet as will permit one member, and as able a man as can be got, to have charge of immigration, to devote his whole time and attention to it. I think it is a job for one man, and I do not believe that any man, I do not care how able, how devoted and how self-sacrificing he is, can ever cany on another department with the Department of Immigration. The work imposed on cabinet ministers by our system is onerous. They have a great deal of departmental work to attend to, a great deal of routine to look after, both in session and out of session, and for four or five months they have to spend a large portion of their time in this House. What we want to do is to set a man apart with the responsibilities of a minister who will think this question out. In this regard I

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
should like to make a few suggestions. I should like the man who is charged with immigration to realize that an immigrant is not only a potential producer, a competitor in the market of producers, he is also a potential consumer, and the fact that there is danger of him becoming unemployed should not have too much weight. Let us get in people strong of brain and strong of body, and let us give them a chance. That is the way to work out the salvation of this nation, because we are going to have hard times in Canada unless we can at least within the next few years substantially increase our population. I want to see the development of a national spirit, and I believe that the more we develop a national spirit the better type of immigrant will we induce to some to this country. I should like to see the abolition of the technical rules which even yet to a certain extent obtain in the department, in order that men may come in more freely. I should like to see use made of our own citizens, no matter from what part of the world they come, in order that they may get into this country friends and relatives who will be useful citizens. I had the pleasure of an instructive trip through the west about fifteen months ago, and I shall never forget as long as I live what one of my hosts said to me when I was visiting in one of the prairie provinces. As he drove me down to the station; he said: "My land marches a mile that way, it goes a mile and a half the other way, and four men and four families could get as good a living off that land as I get now, and there would be four men to pay taxes and four women to help the church organizations and the social life in the country." I think there in a nutshell is our problem. To a large extent we are yet an empty land, and until we fill it up, the burden of the national equipment we possess will hang heavy upon us.
Concerning the railway problem, I am not going to trench upon the ground which has been covered by the member for South York (Mr. Maclean) and the member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), namely, that there should be an amalgamation of some sort between the Canadian Pacific Railway, with their magnificent line of steamers, and the Canadian National Railway. That may be the proper thing to do; I should be glad to study it; but I say meanwhile something has to be done, and I make this suggestion: that the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) should say to the heads of our two great railway companies:	"Gentlemen, cease
useless competition, cease duplication of train services; find out what trains are paying you
and then make arrangements to take off those that are not paying." I think we could save in the tens and twenties of millions of dollars if that policy were adopted. It will not be easy to put into effect, for people do not like to co-operate when they have been competing strongly against each other. But they have got to do it. We cannot allow things to go on as they are, we must elimate useless duplication.

Might I ask a question at that point? Would the hon. member go so far as to suggest that railway rates be reduced until the two companies are compelled to do what he suggests, if they will not do it otherwise?
Mr. MeMASTER: I should not like to hold out the big stick before I had allowed the estimable Minister of Railways and Canals to emulate Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his sunny ways, which I think on the whole would be more likely to bring about the desired result than a display of force. Bu. in all seriousness, the people of this country demand that economy' be the watchword. That does not mean economy merely in little things, it means economy in big things, ana I think the line which I have suggesteu should be followed. For instance, I am told that the competition for business between these two lines is leading at least one of them to altogether too extravagant modes of collecting express shipments. I was told when I went west that in one city in that part of the Dominion where, before the competition had begun, there had been some five engines placing cars in the yards there were now twenty-two. And we all know that throughout the country there are through trains between large cities that could be eliminated. I believe that the people of Canada would be prepared to support any government that showed that it had at heart the interests of the people in the matter of economies in the management of our railways. We must however practise economy ourselves. Two years ago I protested against the tower going up at the present juncture at a further cost of S600,000. But the work was proceeded with and the top has not yet been reached. I do not believe that a government will make any enemies in this country if it shows that it really intends to economize, although I know it is not easy practising economy. I once defined extravagance myself as expenditure on the part of other people of.which we do not approve. So that it is easy to talk economy. But what every member of this House has

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
got to do is to realize himself that he should not ask for his own constituency anything which he does not believe is justified by the financial condition of the country.
I will vote for the budget, not because I am particularly enthusiastic about it; there are features in it which I reserve to myself the right to vote against. But to vote against the budget might mean defeating the government.
Hear, hear.

Well, that "hear, hear" does not commend itself to me; I do not want to see this government defeated. In many ways it is a very good government; for one thing, there has never been any government in Canada in many years which has stood up for the principle of Canadian nationality as this government has done. And that is something that is dearer to me almost than anything else. Burns has said:
Then gently scan your brother man,
Still gentler sister woman;
Tho' thejr may gang a kennin wrang,
To step aside is human: ....
Then at the balance let's be mute,
We never can adjust it;
What's done we partly may compute,

Well, we know what has been resisted; the government has resisted appeals for all sorts of increases in the tariff coming even from constituencies which some of its members represent. And that should be counted to them for righteousness. I will support the government because there have been some reductions in duties. It is true that these reductions are not so many as to tire one in the counting of them; but there have been some reductions on things that should be reduced. My estimable friends in the far corner of the chamber will forgive me if I am candid. They are always so kind and courteous, so smiling and debonair, that it is difficult for one to speak harsh words about them, but at this time one must be outspoken, and must say what is true; our words must be words of truth and soberness. This debate has shown that those hon. gentlemen have no appreciation of the condition of the country. A year or two ago they complained that the Progressives were crape hangers and calamity howlers, but when they themselves got into their stride Alberta, was left nowhere. And with all their statements about the state of things in the country what is their proposal? They propose more taxation, more restrictions; that is the only proposal they have to bring forward. And that same proposal has been made for the last fifty years

and found erroneous. I want to see the government succeed and lead the country along the paths of freedom. We must depend in this country on one school of political thought or the other, and this government will never be really loved by the protectionists; never. Well, I say to the government, be off with the old love and be on with the new.
What about coal?

I have not dissembled my views about coal. Indeed, I have been so frank about coal that I shall be afraid to meet some of my friends from Nova Scotia in the lobby after this speech. I think I hear one of them saying "hear, hear." However, I ask the government-if the trumpet blow an uncertain sound who shall prepare himself for the battle? Personally, I do not want any more uncertain sounds. Restriction has been tried in this country and has failed. Let the government take its courage in both hands and march forward in the ways of reduced duties and it will find itself supported, I believe, by the representatives of the vast majority of the people of this country.

I am somewhat at a disadvantage coming after my eloquent and genial and extremely well informed friend (Mr. McMaster), but I am much indebted to him for some of the things he has dealt with in his speech. Some of them will save repetition on my part. I thank him particularly for what he had to say with regard to agriculture in Canada. What I have to say this afternoon will be largely in the interests of agriculture and particularly in the interests of western agriculture. While I could follow my hon. friend in most of his statements and while I agreed with him on a good deal of what he has advocated with regard to the tariff in particular, I am sorry to say that I cannot at this time see my way clear to go the whole way with him and support the budget. What I want to do particularly is to bring before the House the point of view of agriculture with regard not only to the budget but to some of the other more important questions that are agitating the minds of hon. gentlemen and of the people throughout this country to-day.
Perhaps nowhere in the world has a similar number of people been able to produce so much wealth in the same length of time as have the farmers of the prairie provinces, and with that been able to save so little of the proceeds of their labour. One reason for their great production is of course the ease with which the land is brought under cultiva-

The Bugdet-Mr. Steedsman
tion. That coupled with the fertility of the soil has made it possible to raise more grain per man in the prairies than anywhere else in the world. Yet we must realize that wheat, the greatest of all our exportable commodities to-day, is being produced in the prairies at a loss, one year taken with another. Some of the things that are responsible for that state of affairs I intend to deal with as I proceed. Distance from markets where our products are ultimately sold brings up, of course, the question of transportation both by rail and by water. Then again the expensive system of handling and marketing our crops must be considered, such as the many tolls that are charged from time to time for various services rendered. Then again there is the question of the high interest rates that the farmers have to pay, the question of the cost of production, and the high cost of living-these are all matters that enter into this proposition of the production of wheat at a loss.
The question of railway rates, we are told, will be very thoroughly gone into by the House this year. Hence, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to enter particularly into a discussion of that this afternoon. I just want to pomt out, however, in passing, that not only the agriculturists but all the people of western Canada stand solidly behind the Croivsnest pass agreement rates, and any attempt to interfere with those established rates on grain and grain products wrill be most strenuously opposed I think by all the people of the prairies.
With regard to the rates on the lakes, this was touched on the other day by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston). Perhaps there has been no other service for which we have had to pay more than the service on the lakes. At times the rates have been out of proportion, and I would just like to suggest to the government that if at any future time there is any apparent approach to discrimination against Canadian shippers, they should at once apply the remedy they have now in their hands, that of suspending the ;coastal laws:	We believe
that that would result in eliminating such a state of affairs as we had, for instance, two years ago, when the rates went away beyond everything that ivas reasonable.
The matter of the control of ocean rates is also before the House. In regard to that I just wish to say that I trust the committee that has this inquiry in charge, if it does not approve of the Petersen contract, will introduce some other means whereby ocean rates may be brought down. We realize that 121
the rates on beef cattle, for instance, to England are away out of proportion; they are much too high. We realize, too, that unless the rates are brought down, the beef cattle industry of Canada is doomed. In view of the fact that we are shut out of the American market, there is no other country our beef cattle can go to except Great Britain, and we cannot ship them there at a profit under the present rates. Any scheme that will result in the specific lowering of ocean rates not only on cattle but on other products will, if not at too great a cost to the people of Canada, meet at any rate with my approval.
Then as to the cost of .production and the cost of living-and here is where our disappointment, shall I say, with the present budget comes in-last year a reduction was made, a step forward, as it was called, was taken, and in view of the enthusiasm with which those reductions were accepted in this House and in the country as well, I think we were justified in expecting that at least another further step -would be taken this year, and not only in view of the enthusiasm with which that step was accepted by this House and the country, but also because of its enthusiastic reception by some members at least of the cabinet; in view of the fact also that we have the assurance of the Prime Minister himself, or if not his, we have the assurance of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) that no harm was done to the industry the duties on whose products were reduced last year. Let me point out a few of the things on which we think the duties should be lowered -the food, the clothing and the footwear of the people, cooking utensils, heating appliances, and I was going to add coal, but my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) has handled the coal situation so well that I do not propose to touch on that. On these things I have mentioned the prices should be as low as possible to the people of this country. We believe that on these articles at least the duties should be substantially reduced, and should have been reduced in the budget this year.
I should also like to call your attention, Mr. Speaker, ;to the resolution that was debated in this House a few days ago, which had for its object a lowering of the duty on automobiles and motor trucks. There may



The Bugdet-Mr. Steedsman
be those who contend that automobiles are not a necessity to farmers. To those who hold that view, I would like to say that out on the prairie where I come from, where the distances are so great, and where the conditions prevail such as my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) spoke of, where the large towns are far apart, and settlers live at- a great distance from the railways, the post office, churches and so on, the automobile is not only a great convenience but an absolute necessity, and we had reason to hope that the government would accept the suggestion of my hon. friend and lower the duties there. The sale and distribution of automobiles and automobile service is the biggest thing in this city or in any other city in Canada to-day-unless possibly speculation in wheat in one or two cities. We have no fault to find with that, but we think that an industry that can make such a showing in the few short years in which it has been manufacturing automobiles does not require thirty-five per cent duty. I do not think that I would suggest any slashing reductions in the tariff-reductions that would probably demoralize certain industries and might have the effect of interfering with the revenues of the country. Rather I would think we should have a gradual reduction from year to year that would permit of industry adjusting itself to the changed conditions as we went along, a system that would bring us very shortly to that much to be desired condition where we would have a tariff for revenue only, if there is such a thing. I want to say that I am extremely doubtful if any tariff board can decide through inquiry just where or at what point the tariff would produce the greatest revenue. I am of the opinion that we can only find that out by experience; and unfortunately we have never had a government in this country that has been willing to make the experiment in order to discover where that, point is.
The next matter on which I wish to say a few words is that of rural credits. I have already spoken of the high interest rates. It has not been my privilege to read the report of Dr. Tory who has been working on this matter now, for, I think, practically two years, but I have a fair idea of some of the proposals, at least, that will be submitted to the House. I am firmly of the opinion that agriculture cannot carry the interest charges on long term and other loans that we are do not think it can be done. I trust that the called upon to pay at the present time, I government will come to the assistance of the

provinces in order that they may be placed in a position to extend such systems of rural credit as they have undertaken at the present time. - Some of these systems, at least, are very good. In other words, as it stands now, with the 10 per cent discount in operation all sugar, all spirits, all tobacco, can come into this country through United States ports or through Canadian ports on equal terms. The Acting Minister of Finance has referred to what I presume are the results of the 10 per cent discount which has been added to the preference, and I am glad to say that there is substantial evidence that that is having a very beneficial effect. It is satisfactory for the country, and it is additionally satisfactory as furnishing all the argument I need to show that not only does this preference, even a small preference add greatly to our trade, but it is capable of very material: fexpansion. Last year the imports from the United Kingdom under the preferential tariff amounted to 8102,944,427. The imports from the United Kingdom, under the preferential tariff, through United States ports amounted to $811,749, while the imports from the United Kingdom, under the preferential tariff, through Canadian ports, amounted to $102,132,678.
The figures as regards the effect of the 10 per cent discount have already been quoted. The statistics have only been kept during the last year, but notwithstanding that, if you look back over the different years and compare the amounts that have come through Canadian and through United States ports under the preference, when you find that the amount through United States ports has greatly diminished, it is a fair inference, when

The Budget-Mr. MacLaren
the drop was so great and so sudden within the last year or two, that it is due very largely to the 10 per cent discount which has been added. The result is that last year 99.2 per cent of the imports under British preference came through our own ports. I have here the return for eleven months up to February 28 of this year. I think the statement of the Acting Minister of Finance only covered the period up to December. I am now referring to the showing to the end of February of this year, and the total imports from the United Kingdom were $135,430,030; and from the United States $350,635 with the returns for another month of the fiscal year still to come. I take it as fairly clear that the results this year will be even better than those for last year, even although they were particularly satisfactory. I would think no member of this House would ask for it to be otherwise. Surely no hon. member here regrets the ten per cent discount that was given, judging from the results that accrued from it. Satisfactory as it is I think the preference should be carefully considered still further and made use of to the extent that seems reasonable and advantageous to this country. I do not think that every possible exigency is covered by the British preference as it is. I am not arguing at all as to whether the preference is too high or too low, that is not the point. This inducement was offered in order that trade might be done through our own country, but there are some instances that I have mentioned where really the ten per cent discount does not meet the case fairly. It permits of forty-nine millions of imports coming equally well through the United States as through our own ports. I do not mean to say that all such imports are coming to the United States, I know they are not, but there is a considerable amount coming; the least that can be done in the case of imports coming free from overseas into Canada is to insist upon their coming through our own territory.
In the same class I would put the West India agreement, which is a special arrangement between those colonies and Canada for the mutual advantage of each. In the West India agreement it is laid down that the tariff shall not at any time be more than fifty per cent of the duties in the case of importations under the general tariff, but tobacco, cigars, cigarettes and spirits, with the exception of rum, are excepted from the provisions of this agreement. I Would draw the attention of the House to the fact that under the West India agreement preference all or any West Indian products can be brought info this country just as

well through the United States as they can through Canada. There is not a ten per cent discount and, as it stands, there is no discrimination in favour of Canadian ports as compared with United States ports. Under the circumstances the fortunate thing is that we do get so much trade through Canada. The amount of the West India products that come through the United States may be put down as two millions as against something over twenty millions. Let me say here that there is another point to be considered: the figures of the imports through the United States while accurate as to the method of book-keeping do not represent the actual conditions. We will take the case of bananas that has been so well dealt with by my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan). In the case of the importation of bananas into Canada, what country is it charged up against? Not the West Indies although the bananas may come from there; they are credited to the United States. Why? Because they are bought and paid for in the United States. Therefore I would warn hon. members in looking over these figures, and considering the features of the different preferential tariffs, to study the details carefully, otherwise they may get an entirely too favourable opinion of the existing facts. There are, I am informed, many articles imported into Canada as United States exports which are actually the products of other countries. I illustrated that by mentioning the case of bananas from the West Indies.

Then in estimating the balance of trade between Canada and the United States the difference would not be as great as it seems on the surface'-that is in considering simply the difference between the exports and the imports to and from the United States?

I think that is no doubt correct, but I am a little doubtful as to whether the importation of bananas is a very important factor in the question of the balance of trade between Canada and the United States, the figures are so large. What I am pointing out is that looking at the statistics of the imports from the West Indies into Canada they do not actually represent what we are getting from that territory, and to that extent I think the present treaty is at fault. It is essentially a preferential treaty and it is capable of many improvements according to my judgment. I want to draw the attention of the House to article 8 in the Canadian and West India agreement which states:
The governments of any of the colonies aforesaid on giving six months' notice may provide that to be entitled to the concessions granted in articles 5 and 6 the products of Canada shall be conveyed by ship

It may be pleasant for one to be able to have grapefruit at a very low cost, but I should1 like to ask, under what condition could it be considered as a necessity of life. Surely it is a luxury, and I think anyone who wishes to enjoy grapefruit should be prepared to pay a reasonable amount for it, and we shall be interested later on in hearing from the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. -Robb) his grounds for putting grapefruit on the free list. Surely there can be sufficient preference given to the importation of grapefruit from the West Indies to encourage them to come here, and yet not require us to go to the extreme of a free entry. A few days ago we listened with much interest to the report of the commissioner the hon. member from Cumberland (Mr. Logan), which report was well delivered in this House. I thought it was an admirably prepared report. It showed much evidence of the enthusiasm, the assiduity and the energy, with which the hon. member carried out his work. It must be our wish that his efforts shall be successful in increasing the trade with the West Indies. From such experience as I have had, I have no doubt the recommendations in his report in reference to the increase of trade agencies are necessary and essential things to encourage trade. When these offices are opened up, I hope they will not fall into the error that was made in regard to the offices in South Africa, Australia and New Zealand, where the offices are .properly equipped and furnished, but where
the decorations, including the pictures of our Prime Ministers, past and present, goodlooking men as they are, as well as the pictures of Ministers of Trade and Commerce do not add to the trade. That is not what the people want. It is not business. By all means, let them be placed there, but at the same time let us have something illustrating the actual production, the activities, the manufacturing and the natural products of this country. I suggest that when we establish these additional offices and agents in the West Indies a little more care be taken really to make the pictures of some advantage and something worth while.
I am sure from what I know of the West India service that there is need for improvement in the ships. We want more cold storage, better ships, better accommodation, more speed. These things are most desirable. We are not getting the trade which we otherwise would get, because there is a better service via New York. At the same time I know the West Indian trade has been carried on between Halifax, St. John and the West ' Indies for many years. I suppose it goes back to confederation or before, and I know that the people, while they are anxious to improve the service, are most anxious that nothing should be done to break into a well-established route. The hon. member for Cumberland has spoken of the various routes proposed from Montreal, Charlottetown, St. John and Halifax to the West Indies, and has suggested that six boats be employed. To me that sounds rather attractive, but I think one would be wiser not to express an opinion regarding the suitability or feasibility of this proposed service until it has been carefully considered and discussed by men actually in the trade. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I trust that the investigation held last year will be productive of results.
In addition to the British preference and the West Indian agreement, there are others which are somewhat different, but the principle I think is largely the same. For instance, the French treaty of 1922 applied not only to the French colonies but to many other countries, Norway, Switzerland, the Argentine, Denmark, Japan, Russia, Venezuela, and I believe that even Australia comes under that convention. I do not say anything in reference to the French treaty although I believe there are grounds for very grave criticism of the effects of that treaty. But that is not what I am dealing with. The principle introduced in the treaty that I venture to approve of is that which restricts the prefer-

The Budget-Mr. MacLaren
ence to articles coming through our own ports and territory. Then there is the Italian treaty of the same year with a similar provision. Then there is the Belgian and the Netherland treaties which are really on the same basis. They are getting the intermediary tariff I believe, but they are getting an advantage. Imports under these treaties must come to our own ports and must use our own railways, and therefore I say we are on the right line. There may be points here and there which we could improve on. There may be too many imports that are escaping this provision, but in so far as it goes I think the principle is sound.
Then in addition to all these tariffs and these treaties there is what is called the general tariff, and that tariff is a free-for-all. It is free for every country to make use of. Let me mention the countries or most of the countries that come under the general tariff. We have Germany, China, Austria, Brazil, all of South American foreign countries-except Colombia, Venezuela and the Argentine-Mexico, Central America and Spam. These countries, and I think a few other countries, when they wish to import into Canada, pay the general tariff. It is optional whether the imports pass through Canadian or United States ports, or over American or Canadian railways. There are also certain imports from all countries, Great Britain and elsewhere, under the general tariff, and in those cases it is free to them to come by either country.
Neither the country nor the House has heard anything of a definite character from the government in reference to the Australian treaty. I hope that treaty will materialize. I had an opportunity of meeting Australians, New Zealanders and South Africans during the last year, and the report came out then to South Africa that the treaty had been signed and would come into operation. That is a good many months ago. Since then I have had opportunities of sneaking to those in authority, and those in trade in those countries. They were pleased at that information which has not yet been verified, and they are anxious to do business with Canada. The Australians, while most anxious to trade with us, are rather bitterly disappointed at the small amount that we buy from them. The figures are not conveniently at hand, but I think I am right in saying that the Australians buy about twenty times as much from us as we do from them. The New Zealanders buy much more from us, although not as much as the Australians, than we buy from them, and about the same is true of South Africa. I know many

of them feel that we might fairly try to bring such treaties into force so that we might do more business with them, and I urge the minister, if possible, to expedite the Australian treaty. It will be most favourably received in those countries, and I think, if it is a proper treaty, it will be well accepted in this country.
What do I suggest as a result of what I have said? In the first place, I suggest that the British preference do away with the 10 per cent and that, whatever the advantage is, it apply only to Canada. Let it be made what it was originally intended to be, as it was originally drafted. Have the British preference apply to British possessions in the way it does now, but let us require that it be limited to the using of Canadian ports and Canadian railways, and that it shall not apply to products coming through a foreign country.
The second suggestion that I would make is in connection with the West Indian agreement. At the present, moment, I am not aware of any real difficulty in giving six months notice and making the agreement with the West Indies apply in the same way as I propose for the British preference. The West Indies, as a matter of fact, may make use of the British preference if they ohoose, but it is their option to have that special agreement.
My third suggestion is that conditions governing importations from overseas under the general tariff and those in the free list which now can be made through either Canadian or United States ports be changed; that mot necessarily a large advantage, but sufficient advantage to attain the object be given, and that all importations coming from overseas under the general tariff or under the free list have some preference in coming to Canada direct. Of course, in the case of free entries, one could not make any preference unless a bonus were given, nor is it necessary as regards what I am speaking of to change our tariff. If it is put the other way, if there is a higher tariff for goods coming any other way, there is no material difference. The essential principle is that there be a preference and an advantage in dealing with our own country through our sea ports.
That completes all thait I have to say on this subject. In my opinion, a situation is never so bad that it cannot possibly be worse. I feel in this case there is a silver lining to the cloud and the silver lining is the disintegration that is now taking place in the left wing of the Liberal party. I feel that disintegration will spread to the other wing, and then when you have both wings involved

Mr. Speaker, I wish first to congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) upon the budget he has brought down. The fact that the budget has been criticized by the Conservatives on the ground that the tariff is too low and by the Progressives because it is too high will satisfy the clear-thinking people of Canada that he has taken the only true course consistent with our economic conditions. Let us now examine the conditions which our Acting Minister of Finance had in front of him when he brought down this budget. Let us look at the European situation which has a tremendous influence on trade conditions in Canada. Nowhere in Europe have conditions become stabilized. Conditions are now as bad as they were immediately after the war. Our Conservative friends have attributed the Canadian situation to the tariff. Still, if we examine the European situation, we shall find that, notwithstandmg the fact that many of the industrial nations of Europe have raised their tariffs, no stability has been brought to them, and even at the present moment the Herriot government in France finds itself in danger of its political life on account of the imposition of a ten per cent levy upon the wealth of that nation.
Our Conservative friends have also attributed the conditions existing in this country to our immigration policy. During the session of 1923 they were crying out about the exodus to the United States. The Conservative press was also carrying on a propaganda which painted in dismal colours conditions in Canada and in glowing colours the prosperity of our neighbours to the south. As a result hundreds of prosperous families in northern Ontario were induced to migrate to the United States. In proof of what I am stating, I may say that hundreds of those families have since applied to the Repatriation Bureau in Montreal for assistance to return to their homes. What were the conditions which confronted them when they reached the United States? I may say that the population engaged in agriculture in my section of Ontario are largely French Canadians, and generally their families are large. When those people reached the industrial centres of New England the cotton and woollen mills were paying off their employees by the tens of thousands.
Now, are conditions in Canada as bad as our Conservative friends would have the people believe? I have before me the last report made to the shareholders of the Bank of

Concluding, he said:
We in Canada have much to be thankful for. We have our riches in our forests, our fields, our fisheries and in our minerals, also in our mighty water powers and in the industry and ambition of our people. Where is there a country other than the United States where so high a standard of living prevails? A large portion of the community, notably farmers, who at an earlier day knew little of luxury, now have their electric light, telephones, motor cars and radio. We have no

doles, poorhouses are hard to find and, comparatively, there is little unemployment. The United States for the moment possesses a stronger attraction for emigrants from the Old World, but, taking a longer view, Canada still stands out as a land of opportunity. Nowhere else in the world can the desirable settler from Europe find such good land, such cheap land, under such stable conditions of government and so near to great purchasing markets for farm products.
I would call the attention of this House particularly to the figures quoted as to our favourable trade balance. We find that we exported agricultural and animal products to the value of $619,000,000. It will be seen that in order to have a balanced budget, in other words, a prosperous country, agriculture first of all must be made prosperous. It is Canada's basic industry and it is useless for the apostles of protection to think that Canada can be made prosperous unless the farmer is first given an opportunity of enjoying the same privileges and the same standard of living that obtain in the United States to-day. And how can that be obtained with the policy preached by hon. gentlemen opposite who demand an increase in the tariff? Will that benefit the farmer who has to find a market in Europe for the large surplus of his production? This is no complex question of economics; looked at from the point of view of the ordinary business man, it requires no deep study to realize that the manufacturer in the east depends wholly upon the prosperity of the western farmer. We often hear on this side of the House that the high protective tariff has made the United States prosperous. But, Mr. Speaker, there is now a new point of view; after one hundred and fifty years, of protection the United States to-day has reached the stage where the wheat grower and the cotton grower are told that they must cease production, that the time has come when the United States, owing to economic conditions in Europe, must become a self-contained country consuming its own production and producing for its own consumption. This is the view taken by leaders of the Republican party in the United States to-day. I have here a report of the Coolidge Agricultural Commission which is to be made public in the United States in a few days and from which I shall read a few extracts. I am now quoting .Mark Sullivan in his report to the New York Herald-Tribune:
Any one who follows closely the current developments in government and business in America must recognize the beginnings of this trend. An essential part of the trend is that government and business, including agriculture, agree upon it. This sympathetic cooperation is itself a definite condition of the era on which we are entering. The purpose of it, as yet, is partly instinctive and not fully defined even in the minds of all the leaders of it. But it is apparent that the

government and practically all lines of business in the United States are coming together in an impulse of mutual self-protection to meet the conditions of world-trade arising out of the economic rehabilitation of Europe and its increasing activity.
The policy which America is moving toward, as yet gropingly, is one of withdrawing to itself, making itself a self-contained country, and trying to maintain our high standard of living by avoiding the competition of Europe, in either the role of buyer or of seller. A fairly certain result of that policy should express itself in advocacy of a tariff that will be protective beyond the previous standards of protective tariffs.
The recommendations of the Agricultural Commission include this: "The American farmer can neither compete with imported agricultural products. . . nor can he compete in foreign markets for the sale of his products at world price-levels, created by foreign wrages and standards of living. This means that the American farmer is to get out of Europe, both as a buyer and as a seller. That policy runs counter to the former farm leadership which looked to the revival of Europe as a revival of the market for American farm products.
Running parallel to this, and implied in it, is the theory that the American farmer should at once have complete protection for his own products, and also be tolerant of complete protection for everybody else, the whole looking to a high standard of living for everybody in America.
It is inherent in the policy the Agricultural Commission recommended that the high standard of living in America, both for farmers and for everybody else, be kept secure by a tariff on manufactures sufficient to safeguard America against competition from abroad. This, too runs counter to what has been the teaching of some farm leaders for years past, that the tariff on manufactures should be revised downward so as to bring about lower prices for what the farmer buys.
This new policy proposed by the Agricultural Commission looks to two ends. One is that the American farmer should cease to raise more of any commodity than he can sell in America. To many farmers it will come as a startling suggestion that they should cease, for example, to raise wheat for export. The cotton-raising States will be surprized at any* advice to ignore the foreign market, but competent judges in Washington say the rest of the world is already tending to buy less and less of the American cotton crop, and to turn for its supply to countries where it can be raised by lower-priced labor.
This is the situation to-day in the United States. The leaders of political opinion in that country have come to the stage where they are admitting to the world that they can no longer compete against the low wages and standard of living that obtain in Europe. What effect will that have on Canada? Can the Canadian farmer in the west adopt such a policy, or does the Canadian farmer in the west fully realize what is implied in that policy which is now being advocated in the United States? Canada must for the next century be an agricultural country and must depend upon its natural resources and upon its farm products to develop along the lines which all Canadians look forward to. The Liberal party when it came into power four years ago realized the situation, and it would be just as well for us now to analyze the results of four years of administration in

Canada by this government. When the Liberal party came into power it found the country going rapidly into bankruptcy.
